critique.good: Flight identifiers and times remain on one line, the time columns have a balanced rhythm, and destinations wrap into at most two lines. Rows are comparatively easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the Estimated column and leaves Gate and Status offscreen, so passengers must scroll to see the complete departure information.
critique.cause: The 78px Flight and 120px Destination columns preserve comfortable reading, but together with the 98px time columns and 155px allocated to Gate and Status they produce a 550px table.

critique.good: All headers and individual words remain intact, both time columns fit within the initial viewport, and the table requires less horizontal scrolling than r0A.
critique.problems: Every flight identifier wraps between its airline code and number, making the primary scan target harder to recognize. Several destinations also use extra lines, creating a tall, uneven table. Gate and Status still require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 62px Flight column leaves only 41px for text, below the 57px needed for the longest identifier. The 103px Destination column leaves 82px, forcing the longest destination onto three lines.

critique.good: All six columns are initially visible, so the reader can see the full set of departure fields without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Every header breaks, flight and gate identifiers fragment, some times split, and destination and status words break across lines. The resulting tall rows make finding a flight and comparing times difficult.
critique.cause: The 360px allocation gives each column less text width than its longest unbreakable content requires; the 55px Flight, 62px time, and 43px Gate columns are especially damaging to identifiers and times.

critique.good: Flight identifiers and time values remain intact. Destination names wrap at spaces, and the two time columns have a consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the Estimated header and leaves Gate and Status offscreen. Several destination rows are tall, while Paris occupies three lines.
critique.cause: The first three columns use 286px, so the 98px Estimated column extends beyond the 360px viewport. The 110px Destination column is still too narrow to keep longer names on one line.

critique.good: The narrower Destination and Estimated columns save 11px without introducing word splits or increasing row heights. The paired times remain easy to compare.
critique.problems: The Estimated header still meets the viewport edge, and Gate and Status require horizontal scrolling. Destination wrapping produces the same tall rows as r1A.
critique.cause: The 103px Destination column remains wide enough for its longest word but not for several complete names. At 94px, Estimated fits its header in the table, though its right edge falls outside the viewport.

critique.good: The identifying columns and paired times retain the same readable layout as r1B. The wider Status column gives its contents more room.
critique.problems: The extra status width increases scrolling without improving the visible portion or reducing the reported row heights. Gate and Status remain offscreen initially.
critique.cause: Status grows from 89px to 100px, but it is already beyond the viewport and destination wrapping determines the taller rows.

critique.good: The flight identifiers and both time columns are easy to scan, and the time headers remain intact. Destination names wrap at spaces, preserving their words.
critique.problems: Paris Charles de Gaulle occupies three lines, making its row noticeably taller. The initial viewport cuts through Estimated and leaves Gate and Status offscreen, so passengers must scroll to see key boarding information.
critique.cause: The 103px Destination column leaves 82px for text. The 518px total width puts the end of Estimated and both final columns beyond the 360px viewport.

critique.good: The wider Destination column reduces the longest names to two lines and keeps New York JFK on one line. The table has a calmer vertical rhythm, and the headers and identifiers remain intact.
critique.problems: More horizontal scrolling is required than in the other designs. Estimated is cut off earlier in the initial view, weakening comparison with Scheduled, and Gate and Status remain offscreen.
critique.cause: Increasing Destination to 140px brings the table to 555px and shifts all subsequent columns 37px to the right compared with r2A.

critique.good: The narrower time columns bring more of the table into the initial viewport; both time values are visible and the start of Gate appears. Destination words and flight identifiers remain intact.
critique.problems: Scheduled and Estimated split awkwardly across lines, making the paired headings harder to recognize and giving the header excessive height. Paris still occupies three lines, while Gate is cut by the viewport edge and Status remains offscreen.
critique.cause: The 80px and 78px time columns leave too little text width for their headers. Destination remains 103px, and the 484px table still exceeds the viewport.

r0A.idea: Use a spacious scrolling table with matched time columns and room for destination and status phrases to wrap naturally.

r0B.idea: Minimize horizontal scrolling while preserving the longest unbreakable words and giving destinations and statuses room to wrap at spaces.

r0C.idea: Fit the viewport without horizontal scrolling, accepting split headers and words as well as potentially tall rows.

r1A.idea: Keep flight identifiers and both headers for the paired times intact, while trimming Destination and Status from r0A. Destinations and multiword statuses can wrap at spaces; the 528px table reduces scrolling while retaining readable rows.

r1B.idea: Restore enough width for complete flight identifiers in r0B and retain its compact destination and status columns. The 517px table accepts a three-line destination to reduce horizontal travel while keeping identifiers, headers and individual words intact.

r1C.idea: Keep the complete time pair just inside the initial 360px viewport and give Status more room than in the compact option. This 528px table prioritizes finding a flight and comparing its times at first sight, with Gate and Status reached by scrolling.

r2A.idea: Use r1B as the compact intact baseline: it preserves headers and unbreakable content while keeping horizontal scrolling to the smallest of the three designs.

r2B.idea: Give destinations more room to reduce wrapping where possible. This makes rows easier to scan at the cost of more horizontal scrolling and less of Estimated in the initial viewport.

r2C.idea: Narrow the time columns to bring the start of Gate into the initial viewport. This tests whether showing more of the operational columns is worth splitting the Scheduled and Estimated headers.

r3A.idea: Widen Destination moderately from r2A while keeping both time headers intact. Test whether the extra space reduces destination wrapping without incurring all of r2B's scrolling cost.

r3B.idea: Keep Scheduled intact and narrow Estimated enough for its time values, testing whether the full pair of time columns can sit within the initial viewport. This accepts a split Estimated header to improve first-view access.

r3C.idea: Reduce Destination slightly from r2B to test whether its two-line maximum can be retained with less horizontal overflow.

understanding.purpose: Help passengers find a flight and check its departure time, gate and current status.
understanding.reading: Readers scan flight identifiers or destinations to find a row, then read across it; scheduled and estimated times also invite comparison.
groups: Flight and Destination identify the departure.
Scheduled and Estimated are paired times whose differences reveal delays.
Gate and Status give the immediate boarding information.
keep_intact: Flight identifiers, times and gate identifiers should remain readable as complete units.
Status words and column headers should ideally remain intact.
may_wrap: Destination names can wrap at spaces, especially longer airport names.
Multiword statuses can wrap at spaces; rows already made taller by destination wrapping can absorb this.

bad.why: Both time headers split mid-word, making a closely related pair of labels harder to scan.
Estimated splits mid-word while Scheduled stays intact, weakening the hierarchy of the paired time columns.

final.rationale: r3A keeps flight identifiers and time headers intact while giving destinations enough room to stay within two lines. Its narrower destination column achieves the same row heights as r3C and r2B with less horizontal scrolling. The first view still cuts into Estimated, so readers must scroll to see the full time comparison, gate and status.

general: Keep identifiers and headers intact where possible, especially labels for columns readers compare.
Judge column width by its effect on scanning, row rhythm and scrolling together.
specific: A 120px destination column reduces the longest destination to two lines without the extra width used by r3C and r2B.
The Scheduled and Estimated columns form a comparison pair, but both cannot be fully visible alongside Flight and Destination at this viewport width in the preferred design.

final.tradeoffs: The narrower r1B and r2A require less scrolling but give one destination three lines and make several rows taller. Wider alternatives offer more space for destination names but move the time columns farther beyond the initial viewport.
final.uncertain: The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not browser-tested thresholds; changes near a wrapping boundary may alter the result. Designers may reasonably prefer the narrower r1B or r2A if reducing horizontal scrolling matters more than destination wrapping.

A.why: Flight identifiers and times stay intact, and destinations wrap at word boundaries. Gate and status require horizontal scrolling, while the Estimated header reaches the viewport edge.

B.why: All columns fit, but headers, destinations, statuses and times split within words or numbers, making the board difficult to scan.

C.why: Times and destination words remain intact, but every flight identifier wraps and the gate and status columns require scrolling.

D.why: Flight identifiers and times remain intact, but both time headers split within words. The gate is cut by the viewport edge and status requires scrolling.

E.why: Flight identifiers and times stay intact, and destinations wrap at word boundaries. Gate and status require horizontal scrolling, while the Estimated header reaches the viewport edge.

F.why: The wider destination column keeps Paris Charles de Gaulle to two lines, giving the rows a compact, readable rhythm. The Estimated header crosses the viewport edge, and gate and status require scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The images do not reveal the full widths or contents of the columns beyond the right edge, so the total scrolling cost and off-screen wrapping cannot be compared confidently. A and E look identical in the visible area.

A.why: Flight identifiers and times stay intact, and destinations wrap at word boundaries. Gate and status require horizontal scrolling.

B.why: The wider destination column keeps more names together, but pushes more of the estimated-time column beyond the viewport; gate and status also require scrolling.

C.why: All columns fit, but headers, destinations, times and statuses split within words or numbers, making rows difficult to scan.
